findings.text: The 12 gauge points are not at the CAMELS positions that the layer's own 'source' attribute ('CAMELS camels_topo.txt gauge_lat, gauge_lon') and the README ('the 12 gauge points at the CAMELS gauge_lat/gauge_lon') name. lat/lon are the 3-decimal copies of results/data_audit.json (Hyco Creek 36.398, -79.197; camels_topo.txt has 36.39778, -79.19667). The exported points lie 8.8 to 60.4 m (median 44 m) from the camels_topo.txt positions (largest: South Toe, NC 60.4 m; smallest: Leaf River, MS 8.8 m). All 12 are inside their outlines at either position and 'at most 0.63 km' holds at either (0.629 / 0.631 km), but elev_at_gauge_m differs from results/basin_gis.json gauge.elev_m in 9 of 12 basins (Hyco Creek, NC 130 vs 139; NE Cape Fear, NC 8 vs 9; Little River, NC 131 vs 125; Catawba, NC 377 vs 383; Charlie Creek, FL 7 vs 11; Turkey Creek, GA 90 vs 89; French Broad, NC 666 vs 664; South Toe, NC 811 vs 810; SF Holston, VA 563 vs 548) and distance_to_outline_km by up to 0.056 km (South Toe, NC 0.453 vs 0.509). The basin_gis.json note that the gauge cell is at most 12 m above the lowest cell of the basin holds at the CAMELS positions (largest 12 m) but not at the exported points (SF Holston, VA 21 m). The check table and the '12 of 12 basins agree with basin_gis.json' line cover area, mean elevation, forest share and cell counts only, so nothing flagged it. Fix: in code/27_gis_layers.py after the allclose loop (lines 99-100) add B["gauge_lat"], B["gauge_lon"] = topo.gauge_lat.astype(float), topo.gauge_lon.astype(float) (keep the loop with atol=5.1e-4 as the proof that data_audit.json is the same table rounded to 3 decimals), add gauge.elev_m and gauge.distance_to_outline_km against results/basin_gis.json to the check table and to agrees_with_basin_gis, rerun (10 s; the 24 GeoTIFFs, basins_12.geojson and the CSV keep their hashes - the clean rebuild of this review shows it - while basins_12.gpkg, gauges_12.geojson, README.md and gis_layers.json change). Expected afterwards: elev_at_gauge_m = 139, 9, 125, 383, 116, 11, 9, 89, 64, 664, 810, 548 (in the order of the table) and a largest distance of 0.631 km. If the layer is to stay as it is, change the README sentence and the 'source' attribute to 'gauge_lat/gauge_lon of results/data_audit.json, rounded to 0.001 degree (up to about 60 m from camels_topo.txt)' and say that elev_at_gauge_m and distance_to_outline_km therefore differ from results/basin_gis.json.

findings.text: The licence marking of the elevation product does not survive rendering. The URL pattern 'skadi/<N|S><lat>/<N|S><lat><E|W><lon>.hgt.gz' contains three literal '|' that split the Markdown cell: the row has 7 cells under a 4-column header, and a renderer (python-markdown with tables, same rule as GitHub-flavoured Markdown) drops the excess, so the licence column of the elevation row shows 'S><lat>/<N' and its UNVERIFIED text is not displayed; the source text of the README is correct. Also '<N|S>', '<lat>', '<lon>' and the file names elevation_<gauge_id>.tif / landcover_<gauge_id>.tif in the 'used for' cells (lines 54-55) sit outside backticks and are read as HTML tags (shown as 'elevation_.tif'). Fix: where the README rows are written, replace '|' by '\|' in every cell text (or write 'skadi/<N or S>...' inside backticks), put the URL pattern and the two file-name patterns in backticks as the Files table does, and add a check that every table row has the header's number of cells (g5_readme.py of this review does it in 10 lines).

findings.text: distance_to_outline_km is the geodesic distance to the boundary point that is nearest in DEGREE space (nearest_points on unprojected coordinates), not in metres; at 35 N a degree of longitude is 0.8 of a degree of latitude, so the value can be longer than the true minimum: by up to 13 m here (Catawba 0.200 vs 0.192 km). The README's 'at most 0.63 km' is unaffected. Fix (optional): find the nearest point in EPSG:5070 or a local azimuthal projection, or say 'about'.

findings.text: 'the exported files inherit whatever terms their sources carry' is a legal assumption rather than a recorded fact. It asserts no licence, which is what the rule asks, but 'are derived from sources whose terms are not recorded here' says only what is known.

Both files carry the deprecated 'crs' member (urn:ogc:def:crs:OGC:1.3:CRS84) and every exterior ring is clockwise (0% counter-clockwise), while RFC 7946 asks for counter-clockwise exterior rings and dropped the 'crs' member; Leaflet, geojson.io and QGIS read the files as they are. Coordinates are multiples of 1e-7 degree and equal the GeoPackage within 5e-8 degree (rounding), attributes identical. Optional fix: write with RFC7946=YES.
The area and elevation 'diff' columns print signed zeros ('-0.000000', '+0.0000', 12 rows each, the true differences are about 1e-11 km2 and 1e-13 m). Cosmetic; printing '0' or '< 1e-6' reads better.

findings.where: README 'Known difference' paragraph (the three mountain basins), results/basin_gis.json notes
findings.text: The sentence is stated as in results/basin_gis.json and its figures reproduce (median +1.6 m; DEM mean 8.4 m from the outline file's own elev_mean field on average, largest -24.7 m South Toe; 920 m averaging moves the mean by at most 2.5 m; rank correlation 0.99; the four mountain basins stay above 600 m). One more fact the layers already hold supports it: the shapefile's own elev_mean field for the three basins is 661.7, 976.2 and 1213.3 m against 649.1, 963.3, 1188.5 m from the DEM and 602.2, 863.2, 1025.7 m in camels_topo.txt, so the camels_topo.txt column is the odd one out in these three basins, not the DEM. No change needed; the README may add this line (column outline_file_elev_mean_m).

Against the reviewer's own 15-arc-second buffer (shapely buffer, 64 segments per quarter circle) 549 cells in all (13 to 106 per basin, 0.003 to 0.013% of the valid cells) are nodata in the export and 2 valid cells lie outside it; that is the round-join discretisation of the buffer at the ring edge (all cells inside the outline are valid and equal the source tiles). No action.

verdict_text: Everything the export computes from the data reproduces: the 12 outlines are the source geometry (10 exactly, 2 after the buffer(0) repair, with the shapefile's own AREA unchanged); planar areas in EPSG:5070 equal the attribute to the last digit and results/basin_gis.json to 1e-11 km2; the mean elevations of the cells whose centre lies inside the outline (cos-latitude weighted, found with an algorithm different from the export's rasteriser) equal the attribute to the last digit and results/basin_gis.json to 5e-13 m, with identical cell counts (8,930,167) and no voids; the forest shares equal the attribute to the last digit and results/basin_gis.json to the last digit, with identical cell counts (7,912,882); every exported elevation sample equals the source tile sample and every land-cover cell equals the cached NLCD cell; the README's three check tables equal results/gis_layers.json check_table and the recomputation cell by cell; the three mountain basins (+47, +100, +163 m) are stated as in results/basin_gis.json; a clean rebuild reproduces the sha256 of the 27 deterministic files; the disclosure line is present; the export folder was not touched by the review. Two things are not right. (1) The gauge points are the 3-decimal rounding of the CAMELS positions (8.8 to 60.4 m off), not the camels_topo.txt positions that the README and the layer's source attribute name, and their elev_at_gauge_m differs from results/basin_gis.json in 9 of 12 basins; the check table does not cover the gauges. (2) In the rendered README the licence column of the elevation row is lost (literal pipes inside the URL pattern split the table row), so for one of the three products the UNVERIFIED mark is invisible; the source text is right. A third item is wording (the citation sentence). The gauge fix needs a rerun of the script (the 24 rasters, basins_12.geojson and the CSV keep their hashes); the other two are text fixes in the script's README template. With the three items fixed (or the gauge rounding stated in the README and the source attribute instead of fixed) nothing else needs to change and the verdict would read 'layers hold with wording fixes' at most; run_checks.sh repeats every check in about 40 s, so a second round is cheap.
